query: Which material can be used for improve the magnetocaloric properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A high‐entropy alloy (HEA) that incorporates predominantly magnetic elements (such as Co, Ni, Fe, and Mn) can be used to improve magnetocaloric properties by virtue of its high configurational entropy, which broadens and tailors the magnetic phase transition and enhances magneto‐elastic coupling.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic, single-phase FCC (or near‐FCC) structure HEA (e.g., the well‐known CoCrFeMnNi 'Cantor alloy') in an as-cast or processed state.
generation.intervention: Design and synthesize an HEA with a multicomponent magnetic composition, possibly tuning by adding a minor interstitial element or adjusting composition to optimize exchange interactions.
generation.conditions: Measurements conducted under controlled ambient to cryogenic temperature cycling with applied magnetic field variations typical of magnetocaloric testing.
generation.structural_mediator: The high configurational entropy of the HEA that stabilizes a disordered single solid-solution phase, leading to a tunable distribution of local magnetic environments.
generation.mechanism: The chemical disorder creates a broad magnetic phase transition and potentially enhanced magneto-elastic coupling, which can translate into a larger magnetic entropy change under a magnetic field change.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increased magnetocaloric effect (i.e., a larger magnetic entropy change) relative to conventional magnetic refrigerant materials, although the exact magnitude remains uncertain.
generation.baseline: Conventional magnetocaloric materials such as Gd or other rare-earth based alloys.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected in alloys where the magnetic ordering temperature is suitably adjusted by the alloy composition and remains effective over the desired operating temperature range; extreme disorder or unwanted secondary phases could negate the benefit.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the magnitude of the magnetocaloric enhancement and the potential impact of magnetic hysteresis or reduced saturation magnetization due to disorder; further experimental validation is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the proposed magnetic HEA (e.g., an optimized CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy) and characterize its magnetocaloric properties. Perform systematic measurements of magnetic entropy change (ΔSM) and adiabatic temperature change (ΔTad) across the magnetic phase transition under varying applied fields. Compare the results directly with those of a standard magnetocaloric material (such as pure Gd) under identical conditions.
measurements: Magnetization vs. temperature under different magnetic field strengths
Direct measurement of ΔTad using an adiabatic calorimeter
Calculation of ΔSM from isothermal magnetization curves using the Maxwell relation
Characterization of microstructure and phase homogeneity via XRD and TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured magnetic entropy change and adiabatic temperature change of the HEA are not statistically higher than those of the baseline magnetocaloric material under similar operating conditions, or if the enhanced magnetic response cannot be reproduced reliably, then the hypothesis that the high-entropy design improves magnetocaloric properties will be falsified.

The appearance of high entropy alloys breaks the traditional design concept of alloys based on mixing enthalpy and opens up a broad space for composition design for the research and development of new materials. The comprehensive effect of the mixing of various main elements endows the high entropy alloy with high entropy effect in thermodynamics, lattice distortion effect in structure, hysteresis diffusion effect in dynamics, and “cocktail” effect in performance [ [1] , [2] ]. The principle of multi-principal element design based on these four effects results in the high entropy alloy showing many unique properties beyond the traditional alloy. These characteristics cover excellent corrosion resistance [ [3] ], wear resistance [ [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] ], excellent fatigue strength, and yield strength under various temperature conditions [ [10] , [11] ], high hardness [ [12] ], excellent microstructure stability and thermal stability [ [13] , [14] ], and excellent high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [15] ]. High entropy alloys (HEAs), complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), and multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are the most common names of a new group of materials [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ] introduced by Yeh et al. [ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. A new approach to HEA design using the valence electron concentration (VEC) was recently proposed with the aim of increasing the plasticity of these alloys [ [10] , [11] ].
